item.title: 5-5 Norms vs. laws vs. markets
item.description: Part of 5 Act IV — The Coordination Problem (us)Most coordination problems arrive with three candidate answers, and they are not three flavours of the same thing. Who gets the scarce lane at 8 a.m. can be settled by a queueing convention, by a traffic statute, or by a toll. Whether a river stays fishable can be settled by shared practice, by a regulator, or by a market in catch quotas. A norm, a law, and a market each make strangers behave predictably — but they use different detectors, different sanctions, different information, and they fail in different ways. Choosing among them is one of the few genuine design decisions available inside a complex system, and almost every real arrangement turns out to be all three stacked on top of one another.All three answer the same four questions: what is the expected behaviour, who notices deviation, what happens on detection, and what does the apparatus cost to run. The differences show up in the third and fourth columns, and they are large.The deepest asymmetry is in the detector. A norm needs observability: if nobody sees the behaviour, there is no one to enforce. A law needs legibility: a rule that cannot be stated generally and proved afterwards cannot be enforced, however desirable it is — which is why the tacit knowledge that makes an organisation actually work tends to fall outside both the statute and the contract. A market needs neither, because no one has to notice anything: the cost lands directly on the person who incurred it, through the price.Norms are emergent order in its purest form. Nobody drafts them; they accumulate from repeated interaction and are enforced by whoever happens to be present. Enforcement is usually second-party (the person you inconvenienced) or third-party (a bystander who has no stake in this particular case), and its currency is reputational rather than material: disapproval, gossip, the withdrawal of cooperation, exclusion from the group.That design has two enormous advantages. It is nearly free in the common case — the sanction is a look, and the deterrent is the anticipation of one — and it is extraordinarily fine-grained. A norm can encode local conditions that no rule-writer could enumerate: when queueing is expected, how much noise is acceptable at what hour, which seats you offer to whom. This is the tacit knowledge that formal systems keep failing to capture.The conditions are as important as the benefits. Norms hold where behaviour is observable, where the parties expect to deal with each other again (the shadow of the future), and where the group broadly shares expectations about what is normal. Strip any of those out and enforcement evaporates. This is why norms govern village water use and not anonymous littering on a motorway: in the one-shot interaction with a stranger, there is no reputation to lose and nobody to lose it to.Norms also fail in ways that are less discussed. They can be genuinely oppressive — many of the most costly norms in history were the ones allocating status, who belongs, and who may speak. They are path-dependent, so they can persist long after their reason has gone, and because they are inherited rather than written they are easy to mistake for human nature. And they resist deliberate change: you cannot legislate a norm, though you can sometimes legislate conditions in which one grows. What you can also do is destroy one, usually by accident.Law is a made order — deliberately constructed, oriented to a stated purpose, held together by commands and the credible threat behind them. Its great advantage over the norm is that it works where norms cannot: between strangers, across one-shot interactions, at scale, and against harms that fall on third parties who were never part of the transaction. The owner of the paper mill does not need to be shamed by his neighbours, and his downstream neighbours do not need to negotiate with him repeatedly. They need an authority that will make him stop.Three further advantages are worth naming. Law can be prospective, letting people plan against rules that exist before they act. It can function as a commitment device, binding the state or the public to a course that would otherwise be abandoned the moment it became inconvenient. And it produces dispute resolution that does not depend on the parties continuing to like each other.The costs are equally structural. Enforcement is expensive and capacity is finite, which means every statute is in competition with every other for inspectors and court time. Law is slow to update relative to the conditions it governs. It is vulnerable to capture — the regulated usually have the strongest incentive to shape the rules, and the most resources with which to do it. And it decays under measurement in exactly the way the Goodhart discussion describes: police judged on arrest counts, regulators judged on fines levied, agencies judged on cases closed, all gradually optimising the number they can see instead of the outcome they were built to produce.Above all, law depends on legibility. Writing a rule requires reducing a situation to terms that a general reader can apply and a court can verify. Whatever cannot survive that reduction is invisible to the statute — and so, very often, is the very thing that made the practice work.Markets coordinate without anyone agreeing about what is worth wanting. That is their distinctive trick. Buyers and sellers who share no values, no language, and no intentions can still transact, because the only thing that has to be mutually intelligible is the price. And the price is a compression: a single number summarising scarcity, demand, and the local knowledge of thousands of people who never report to anyone — the mechanism explored under emergent versus designed order.The information advantage is the one to hold onto. A market does not need to collect dispersed knowledge, only to transmit a signal about it, and each participant acts on their own private circumstances without explaining themselves to a centre. Its detector is automatic: nobody has to notice your error, because the loss arrives regardless.Its failures are equally precise, and they all have the same shape — the signal is missing where nothing can be owned: Externalities. Costs that land on people outside the transaction, who cannot charge for them: pollution, noise, congestion, a depleted aquifer. Public goods. Things that are costly to provide and impossible to exclude from, so nobody's private incentive covers the cost. Common-pool resources. Rivalrous but hard to fence — the subject of the tragedy of the commons and of Ostrom's escape from it. Asymmetric information. When one side knows more about the thing being sold, the price stops clearing the market honestly. Two further limits matter as much. First, markets need law and norms to function at all: property, contract, courts, credible money, and a background expectation that most people will not simply defraud you. Second, the allocation a market produces follows willingness to pay, and willingness to pay tracks wealth. That is a value choice presented as an emergent outcome — the is/ought gap with a price tag attached.Read the stack upwards and it explains why the three are not substitutes in any simple sense. A market cannot exist without enforceable property and contract. A legal system cannot function on coercion alone, because enforcement capacity is finite and most compliance in any functioning society is voluntary — a law nobody believes in is a surcharge on the honest. And the norms at the bottom are the ones markets and statutes quietly consume.They also eat into each other. The best-known demonstration is the daycare study: a group of Haifa childcare centres introduced a small fine for parents who collected their children late. Lateness rose rather than fell, and — the part that matters — it stayed high after the fine was withdrawn. The explanation is a change of frame: a lateness that was a breach of consideration toward a person became a service purchased at a listed price, and parents optimised against the price. Withdrawing the price did not restore the norm, because the reframing did not reverse. The same argument runs through Titmuss's case against paying blood donors. One caveat, in keeping with everything this book has said about single studies: the effect is widely cited, the replications are mixed, and the honest reading is that the mechanism is credible and its magnitude unsettled. Treat it as a live hypothesis to test in your own context, not a law of nature.One scarce resource, three possible regimes. Norm. First-come-first-served, with a body of tacit merging etiquette — let one car in, don't block the junction, don't use the shoulder. Nearly free to run, and it degrades gracefully under light load. It collapses at saturation, when nobody can see who arrived when and every driver can plausibly claim priority. Law. Right-of-way rules, signals, a bus lane with a penalty, a box junction you may not enter. Costs inspectors and cameras, works among strangers, and can reserve capacity for people who were never going to win a queue — which is itself a value judgement written into the rule. Market. Congestion charging, tolled express lanes, priced parking. Clears the lane and raises revenue, allocates strictly by ability to pay, and generates a political problem with a familiar shape: the losers are concentrated and identifiable, the winners are diffuse. Notice that all three settle the same question — who gets the space — and settle it differently. The efficiency question, which clears traffic fastest and at what total cost, is empirical and answerable. The distribution question, who should bear the cost and who should get through, is not settled by any amount of evidence; it needs a bridge premise about what is worth wanting, supplied from somewhere other than the data.There is a second lesson in that example. London's congestion charge works mainly because most drivers pay it voluntarily. The cameras are a backstop, not the mechanism; enforcement of a charge against a population that has decided to ignore it is not affordable at any realistic budget. Every market and every statute ultimately stands on a floor of voluntary compliance, which is the bottom layer of the diagram above.The questions that actually decide it: What is the information structure? Dispersed, local, and tacit favours norms and markets. Central, provable, and general favours law. Who can see the behaviour? No observability, no norm. No legibility, no enforceable rule. Who bears the enforcement cost? Norms look free until the group gets large; law is expensive per case and needs a budget. Do the parties disagree about ends or only means? Markets coordinate people who agree on nothing; norms require enough shared expectation to define a violation. Will the mechanism destroy the thing it regulates? Pricing and fining can reframe moral obligations as commercial ones, and the reframing is not cheap to undo. Three practical rules follow. Prefer the mechanism that works at the lowest total cost, including the cost of monitoring it. Expect hybrids, and design them deliberately — a price with a norm underneath and a statute behind it is usually stronger than any one alone. And schedule a review: every mechanism decays, markets attract rent-seekers, laws drift under their own metrics, and norms change in ways nobody announced.When none of the three can be reached — when the only stable arrangement requires everyone to restrain themselves simultaneously and no one can enforce the restraint — the result is a race to the bottom that no participant wants. Law is the usual escape from that trap, which is why the politics of enforcement matters more than the elegance of the design. Coordination mechanism — any arrangement that aligns the behaviour of independent actors; here, norms, laws, and markets are treated as three distinct technologies for doing so. Norm — an unwritten expectation enforced by those present, through disapproval, gossip, exclusion, or lost trust. Law — a formal, prospective, generally stated rule enforced by a specialised authority with coercive power. Market — a coordination mechanism in which behaviour is disciplined by prices, profit, loss, and the ability to exit. Observability — the property of behaviour being visible to those who might sanction it; the precondition for norm enforcement. Legibility — the property of behaviour being expressible as a general, verifiable rule; the precondition for legal enforcement. First-, second-, and third-party enforcement — enforcement by the actor themselves, by the affected party, or by an uninvolved bystander; norms rely mainly on the second and third. Shadow of the future — the expectation of dealing with the same parties again, which makes present defection costly and gives norms their grip. Externality — a cost or benefit falling on someone outside the transaction, who cannot charge for it; the characteristic market failure. Public good — a benefit that is costly to provide and impossible to exclude people from consuming, so private incentives under-supply it. Willingness to pay — the criterion markets allocate by; tracks wealth, and so makes distribution a value question rather than a technical one. Motivation crowding out — the erosion of a norm when a price or fine reframes a moral obligation as a paid transaction. Regulatory capture — the tendency of the regulated to shape the rules that govern them, since they have the strongest incentive and the most resources. Mixed regime — a real arrangement combining all three mechanisms, typically with the market layer resting on law and both resting on voluntary compliance.

item.title: 5-6 Social construction
item.description: Part of 5 Act IV — The Coordination Problem (us)Some things are real because they are made of matter, and some are real because enough people treat them as real. Money, borders, marriage, corporations, race, weekends, and the value of a signature all fall into the second group. This subsection is about that second group — what it means for something to be socially constructed, why the phrase is both indispensable and routinely misused, and how constructions acquire the power to shape a world full of physical things.The practical stakes are high, because the answer to "is this constructed?" is usually assumed to settle "is this real?" or "should we keep it?" Neither follows. Getting the logic right is what lets you see, in the same glance, why a currency can collapse overnight and why no amount of disbelief will let you walk through a wall.John Searle's division is the cleanest place to start.Brute facts are indifferent to your opinion. Institutional facts are made of opinion — but not the opinion of any one person, and not the kind of opinion you can revoke privately.Searle's formula compresses the mechanism into a sentence: X counts as Y in context C. A rectangle of polymerised cotton counts as twenty pounds in the United Kingdom. A person standing in a particular box on a particular day counts as a voter. A group of people filing a document counts as a legal person that can own assets and be sued. The physical substrate is doing something, but it is not doing the important thing.Ian Hacking's The Social Construction of What? (1999) sorted the muddle by noticing that "constructed" answers at least two different questions, and people slide between them mid-sentence.Causal construction. The thing was shaped by social forces — history, power, custom, economics. Almost everything human is causally constructed in this sense. Childbirth practices, maths curricula, and the layout of your city all qualify.Constitutive construction. The thing exists only because of the agreement. Money is constitutively constructed; the fact that a banknote is worth something is not a fact about paper.Both can be true of the same object, and neither implies that the object is unreal, arbitrary, or bad. The word "constructed" is a claim about origin, not about status. This is precisely the same mistake as reading "emergent" as "good" — an origin story doing work that only a value premise can do.Three questions turn the vague phrase into an actual claim: What is the physical substrate? There is always one. There is no construction floating free of matter. What agreement does the thing require? Whose, how broad, how maintained? Is the construction constitutive or merely causal? What would remain if the agreement evaporated? Nobody decided that money would be money, and nobody voted on which side of the road to drive on. Constructions are a coordination phenomenon, and the mechanism is the same one that produces focal points.The essential ingredient is not agreement in the sense of approval. It is common knowledge — I expect it, I expect you to expect it, I expect you to expect me to expect it. That mutual expectation is what makes the behaviour self-sustaining without any enforcer.This is why pointing out that something is constructed almost never changes it. The construction does not rest on your belief; it rests on everyone's expectation of everyone's behaviour. Explaining to a queue that the queue is a mere convention does not dissolve the queue.Two corollaries follow. First, constructions can be designed — time zones, patents, the metre — but once adopted they behave like grown order, with all the knowledge-dispersal and adaptation properties that entails. Second, changing a construction requires changing what people expect others to do, which is a coordination problem, not an argument. That is where law, mandate, focal events, and shocks come in — the same toolbox that gets a locked-in standard unstuck.What makes institutional facts special is that they do not merely describe; they assign. Searle calls these deontic powers: rights, duties, permissions, obligations, authorisations.Notice the loop closing. The powers are real because people act on them; people act on them because the powers are real; and the loop is stabilised by a shared expectation rather than by force, though force is often available as a backstop. Declarations are the act that starts the loop — "I pronounce you…", "I resign", "the meeting is adjourned" — a speech act that changes the world rather than describing it.This is the connection to legibility. States are in the business of manufacturing institutional facts at scale: surnames, cadastral maps, standard weights, identity documents, official categories. These are not neutral descriptions of what was already there; they are instruments that make a population administrable, and they reshape the people they classify.Start with the substrate. A banknote is a printed slip. Apply the formula: X (this slip) counts as Y (a claim on real goods) in C (the issuing jurisdiction and its trading partners).Now ask the diagnostic question — what happens if everyone stops believing? Everything. Nothing about the paper changes; the purchasing power is gone. Hyperinflations are this happening in real time. The Weimar marks, the Zimbabwean dollars, and the Venezuelan bolívars were not destroyed; the mutual expectation collapsed, and the substrate was revealed as substrate.But do not over-read the lesson. The construction is not arbitrary. It is backed by things that are far less constructed: the state's power to tax in that currency, productive capacity, the willingness of armed people to enforce contracts. Meanwhile some of the most consequential constructions in finance are ones nobody consciously agreed to. A credit rating is a status function assigned by a private agency, which then triggers regulatory rules that treat the rating as a fact about risk — powers, in Searle's sense, granted by an agreement nobody remembers making. In 2008 the loop turned violent in the ordinary direction: when enough participants stopped expecting the AAA designation to mean what it said, the designation stopped meaning it, and assets priced on the assumption had to be repriced.Before 1883, "noon" meant the moment the sun crossed the meridian where you stood. That was a brute fact about astronomy, and it worked fine until railways made it possible to travel far enough, fast enough, for the discrepancy to matter. Rail timetables in the United States listed dozens of local times, and near-simultaneous trains could collide because two stations disagreed about what time it was.On 18 November 1883, American railroads imposed standard time by fiat — five zones, one day, announced rather than legislated. Congress ratified it in law in 1918. Within a generation the convention felt natural.Look at what happened. A coordination problem (everyone needs to mean the same thing by "3 p.m.") was solved by a focal solution (the railroads), adopted because non-adoption was worse, and then hardened into a fact nobody experiences as a choice. Today, jet lag is a real physiological symptom of an administrative decision, and no individual can opt out. The construction is not less real for being constructed — it is in your body.This one shows why the crude version of the concept fails. Race is not a biological taxonomy: human genetic variation is clinal and does not partition into the folk categories. But race is not therefore nothing.Three distinct claims are usually tangled together, and separating them is the whole exercise: The classification is constructed. "Black" and "White" as mutually exclusive administrative boxes were assembled historically through slavery, colonialism, census categories, and law (the one-drop rule is a construction visible in the plumbing). The consequences are brute. Exposure to discrimination, differential policing, environmental burden, wealth gaps, and stress physiology produce real, measurable differences in health. Racism is a physical exposure. The clinical shortcuts built on it were bad medicine. Race-based algorithms — the eGFR kidney-function correction, spirometry reference values, some risk scores — treated a social category as a biological parameter. A 2021 task force convened by the National Kidney Foundation and the American Society of Nephrology recommended removing the race coefficient from eGFR estimation, and similar corrections have been dropped elsewhere. The lesson is not "race is fake, so ignore it." It is that a constructed category can carry enormous causal weight, and can also be a bad proxy for the thing you actually want (ancestry, exposure, circumstance) — and that the only way to tell which is happening is to ask what work the category is doing.This is Hacking's looping effect at work: classifications of people are not indifferent to the people classified. Apply a label, build institutions around it, and people respond to the label — forming identities, adjusting behaviour, generating new statistics, which then appear to confirm the label.Because constructions run on belief and behaviour, they can be made true by being believed — or made false by the attempt to prevent them. The Thomas theorem states the general case: situations defined as real are real in their consequences.A bank is solvent as long as depositors expect it to be; a rumour that it is not turns it insolvent, which then confirms the rumour. A rating of a neighbourhood as high-risk raises the cost of credit there, which suppresses investment, which produces the conditions the rating predicted. A school labelled failing loses the pupils whose parents can move, which makes it fail.The mirror image matters too. A published forecast of a shortage can cause hoarding, or can cause conservation. A credible warning of a riot can cause police mobilisation that prevents it, so the prediction looks like a false alarm. Constructions do not just sit there being believed; they are inputs to the systems described elsewhere in this act.The concept is powerful and therefore attracts sloppy use. Four failure modes are worth naming explicitly, because catching them is most of the skill."Constructed, therefore arbitrary." Constructions are contingent — they could have been otherwise — which is not the same as random or unmotivated. Standard time solved a real problem. Money solves a real problem. Language solves a real problem. Contingency tells you the thing is a choice, not that it is a bad one."Constructed, therefore unjust." This is the is/ought gap wearing a lab coat. That something was assembled by historical forces is a descriptive claim; that it should be dismantled is a normative one, and it needs a bridge premise. Note that the bridge usually exists and is usually reasonable — but it must be stated, because otherwise the argument is doing an illegitimate slide, and it loses against anyone who shares your facts but not your values."Constructed, therefore changeable by explanation." Pointing out that a construction is a construction changes nothing, because it was never resting on individual belief. Constructions change when expectations change — via mandate, focal event, incentive redesign, or collapse — which is coordination work, not rhetoric."Everything is constructed." If the word applies to everything, it discriminates nothing. The test is the disbelief experiment: stop everyone believing, and see what survives. Gravity, arsenic, and the tide survive. Money, weekends, national borders, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average do not. And note that many of the most interesting cases are mixed — race, disease categories, "intelligence", wilderness — where a substrate is real but the boundaries are drawn by us.The last row points at a subtle and important asymmetry. Some constructions are ontologically shallow — a fad, a hashtag — and some are ontologically deep, having been layered into law, capital, bodies, and habit over centuries. Depth is why dismantling a shallow construction takes a fortnight and dismantling a deep one takes generations, even when everyone agrees it should go. That is path dependence applied to meanings.Strip the misuse away and social construction does four jobs that nothing else in this act does.It explains how order emerges without a designer. Constructions are the mechanism by which coordination happens among people who never met — a genuinely grown order with a deontic edge.It explains why institutions have teeth. Rights, duties, and authority are not physical forces, yet they move armies. Searle's answer — status functions assigning deontic powers — is the bridge between coordination and the machinery of institutions.It supplies the origin story for genuine constraints. Social constructions, once deep enough, behave like brute facts for everyone inside them. The price of bread, the value of a degree, the seriousness of a criminal record: none are physical, all are binding.And it supplies the diagnostic vocabulary for asking what is contingent. "Which of the constraints on my options are physics, and which are agreements?" is one of the highest-yield questions available, and it is unanswerable without this distinction. Most things that feel like laws of nature are agreements that outlived the people who agreed.When you meet the phrase in the wild — from a colleague or from yourself — run this: What is the substrate? Name the physical thing or act underneath the status. Who must agree, and how do they know the others agree? Find the common knowledge. Constitutive or merely causal? Run the disbelief test. What powers does it assign? Rights, duties, permissions, authorisations — the deontic layer. How deep is it? Weeks to change, or centuries? What has been built on top? What is it doing that something else could do better? A category can be constructed, consequential, and still a bad proxy for what you care about. If you want it changed, what is the coordination mechanism? Mandate, incentive, focal event, or collapse. Argument alone is not on the list. Question 6 is the one that turns the concept from a debating weapon into an instrument. The useful version of "X is socially constructed" is never the bare observation. It is the follow-up: constructed out of what, held up by whom, doing which work, and replaceable with what?Social construction — A thing that exists or has its character because of widespread agreement, expectation, and practice, rather than because of its physical properties alone.Brute fact — A fact that holds independently of anyone's beliefs; the class against which constructions are contrasted.Institutional fact (Searle) — A fact created by assigning a status to something that carries powers; the formula is "X counts as Y in context C."Status function — The assignment by which a physical thing or act takes on a social role — a slip of paper counting as money, a person counting as a judge.Deontic powers — The rights, duties, permissions, and authorisations that a status function confers, and which thereby change behaviour.Causal construction — The claim that a thing was shaped by social and historical forces; true of nearly everything human, and not by itself a claim about its reality.Constitutive construction — The stronger claim that a thing exists only by agreement, so that dissolving the agreement dissolves the thing.Common knowledge — The condition in which everyone knows, and knows that everyone knows, and knows that everyone knows that everyone knows; the ingredient that makes a convention self-sustaining without enforcement.Looping effect (Hacking) — The process by which classifying people changes them, so that the classified respond to the label and generate evidence that appears to confirm it.Self-fulfilling prophecy (Merton) — A belief that produces the behaviour which makes the belief true; the Thomas theorem ("situations defined as real are real in their consequences") is its general statement.Ontological depth — How far a construction has been layered into law, capital, bodies, and habit; deep constructions behave like brute facts for those inside them and resist rapid change.Disbelief test — The diagnostic of asking what would happen if everyone stopped believing in a thing: nothing survives for brute facts, everything for constitutive ones, and something for mixed cases.Mixed case — A thing with a real substrate and socially drawn boundaries — race, disease categories, "intelligence" — where the substrate is not negotiable and the boundaries are.Ontological gerrymandering — Declaring other people's beliefs to be constructed while presenting one's own analysis as neutral description; a rhetorical move that immunises the analyst's claims from the very treatment they apply to others.Reification (of a construction) — Treating an agreement as a natural fact; the mirror error of treating a natural fact as an agreement, and the one that makes contingent arrangements look unchangeable.

item.title: 5-7 Moloch - multipolar traps
item.description: Part of 5 Act IV — The Coordination Problem (us)A multipolar trap is a situation in which everyone involved would prefer a different outcome, everyone involved is doing something entirely reasonable, and the outcome is bad anyway. Its defining feature is the absence of a villain. Nobody has to be greedy, shortsighted, or malicious for the trap to close; the participants can describe the structure perfectly and still be unable to leave it. Once you can see this shape, you find it everywhere — in antibiotic resistance, exam prep, advertising, fisheries, litigation, arms races, and the thirty seconds before every meeting where somebody proposes a new metric.Start with the smallest version, the prisoner's dilemma. Two players each choose to cooperate or defect; the payoffs are:Whatever B does, A does better by defecting — defect against a cooperator and you get 5 instead of 3; defect against a defector and you get 1 instead of 0. The move is dominant. The same reasoning runs for B, so both defect, and the pair lands on (1, 1). Yet both would clearly have preferred (3, 3). The outcome is a Nash equilibrium — nobody can improve by changing strategy alone — and it is simultaneously Pareto-dominated, meaning everyone could be better off at a different outcome.That gap between "no one can move" and "everyone would prefer to move" is the whole phenomenon. Three ingredients produce it: A competitive margin. Something is being contested — a resource, a rank, a market, a mate, a vote — and effort placed on that margin buys an advantage. An uninternalized externality. The cost of your move lands somewhere other than on you: on other users of a shared resource, on your rivals' customers, on strangers, or on the future. If the cost did land on you, the market would handle it. No ability to contract your way out. The parties either cannot agree, cannot trust each other's promises, or cannot verify compliance. That last point is where Ronald Coase's insight bites: externalities are fundamentally a bargaining failure. When the affected parties are few, well defined, and able to write and enforce an agreement, they will usually fix the problem themselves — the polluter and the downstream fishermen can strike a deal. When the parties are numerous, anonymous, and unable to check whether anyone is cheating, they cannot, and the trap holds. Every escape route in this chapter works by attacking one of the three ingredients.The label multipolar comes from Nick Bostrom's work on the strategic risks of advanced artificial intelligence, where he used it for competitive scenarios in which each agent is driven toward a course of action it would rather avoid, because any agent that unilaterally restrained itself would simply be outcompeted. The AI context is exotic; the structure is ancient.What the many-player version adds is a ratchet. With two players choosing cooperate or defect, the trap is a one-step collapse. With many players and a continuous variable — how much to spend, how many fish to take, how hard to compete — the level climbs and never comes back down, because at every point along the climb the locally best move is to add a little more.Two features make the ratchet worse than the collapse. First, it is invisible: each individual step is small, defensible, and looks like a normal decision. Second, it is sticky: when pressure eases, nobody steps back down, because stepping down first is exactly the move that was punished on the way up. This is why arms races, ad budgets, and regulatory standards so rarely return to earlier levels even in peacetime, and it is the reason traps are a close relative of path dependence — the level you are at is a residue of history rather than a response to current conditions.Almost every trap you meet is a variation on one of these. The differences matter, because they determine which escape is available.The last one deserves a note, because it is the most common and the least recognized. A positional good is one you value only by comparison — a place at the top school, a house in the good catchment area, a title. Competition for positional goods is a pure ratchet: the total stock of status never increases, so the escalation burns resources without producing anything anyone actually wanted. This is the mechanism behind the education arms race, credential inflation, and the peculiar sensation of running very fast to stay in place. (The best-known trap of all, the depletion of a shared resource, is the commons; it earns its own treatment next.)The cleanest demonstration available is Martin Shubik's 1971 dollar auction, and it fits in a paragraph.An auctioneer offers a $1 bill. Bidding starts at 5 cents and rises in 5-cent increments. The twist: both the highest and the second-highest bidders pay, but only the highest receives the dollar.The trap springs at around 55 cents. The two leading bidders now face a choice that is locally rational and globally absurd: withdraw and lose 50 cents outright, or bid 60 and pay 60 cents for a dollar — which is still, at that instant, a good deal. Both bid. The escalation continues until bids exceed $1, at which point every further bid increases a certain loss in order to avert a larger one. Pairs of rational adults have bid many dollars for a single dollar bill in classrooms, repeatedly, while fully understanding the structure.Three features are worth extracting: The sunk cost is genuine, not imagined. Past bids are unrecoverable, but they change the payoff of quitting now, because quitting converts them from "spent in pursuit of a prize" into "lost." The trap uses a real accounting change, not a psychological error alone. Asymmetry of loss, not hope of gain. Past a certain point, both players are choosing between a small loss and a larger one. Nobody is being greedy; both are minimizing damage. There is no unilateral exit. Either bidder could have declined at the start. Neither can stop the other's escalation, and stopping alone guarantees the loss. Real instances share the anatomy: litigation that both sides would settle if they could coordinate, price wars that destroy an industry's margins, bidding wars for acquisitions, campaign spending, R&D races. In each case, the participants are not confused. They are stuck.The most consequential contemporary example runs on a slow clock, which is why it has been allowed to get this far.Antibiotic resistance is a commons problem with a delay. The resource — the continued effectiveness of a class of drugs — is shared by everyone on the planet and belongs to no one. The move is to use antibiotics generously: prescribe them when a patient pressures you, use them prophylactically in livestock, use broad-spectrum ones because a culture takes two days.Trace the incentives: The benefit is concentrated and immediate. The patient recovers and stops calling. The farm's animals grow cheaper. The prescriber avoids a difficult conversation and a bad review score. The cost is diffuse and delayed. Every unnecessary prescription contributes a tiny increment to resistance, which lands on strangers, decades in the future, through a mechanism no individual can see. Unilateral restraint is actively punished. A doctor who withholds antibiotics today pays the full cost — patient dissatisfaction, and the occasional missed infection — while the benefit to the global commons is imperceptible. The structure pays for overuse and fines restraint. Run the unilateral-restraint test on this and you get a clear verdict: materially punished, with no compensating reward. That is a structural trap, and it is why individual virtue alone has never been a sufficient fix. The available escapes work on each ingredient in turn — stewardship programs and prescribing audits make behaviour visible (reducing transaction costs), a regulatory ban on growth-promotion use supplies an enforcer, rapid diagnostics that distinguish bacterial from viral infection change the arena, professional norms change the payoffs, and "subscription" payment models that decouple drug company revenue from volume attack the incentive at its source.The name most often attached to this family of outcomes comes from outside economics. Moloch was a Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice, mentioned in Leviticus and given a memorable role by Milton in Paradise Lost as the fiercest of the fallen angels. Allen Ginsberg's Howl (1956) turned the name into a one-word indictment of industrial civilisation — "Moloch whose mind is pure machinery!" In 2014, Scott Alexander's essay "Meditations on Moloch" stitched the older literary image to the game-theoretic structure, and the name stuck in a certain corner of the internet.The name earns its place for one reason: it names an outcome without naming a perpetrator. Ordinary causal language is built for agents — someone did this, someone is to blame — and traps break that language. "Who is responsible for credential inflation?" has no answer, and the search for one produces conspiracy theories and scapegoats. "Moloch" is a shorthand that stops that search and points at the structure instead.But the metaphor carries a real hazard, and it is worth stating plainly: Moloch is not an agent. There is no entity with preferences pursuing child sacrifice. The moment the word is used as though it were a force, an explanation, or an excuse, it stops being analysis and becomes a way of saying "the system made me do it." The structure is always just a payoff matrix, an externality, and a set of agents. If you cannot point to those three things, you have not identified a trap; you have invoked a mood.This is also the sharpest demonstration of a point made earlier in this act: emergent order is not salvation. A multipolar trap is a spontaneous order — nobody designed it, nobody wants it, and it is stable. Emergence is a claim about where a pattern came from, never about whether it is good.The concept has a characteristic failure mode in each direction, and they are worth separating because they are often confused.The first is blame-the-villain thinking. Human causal cognition reaches for an agent, so we look for the bad actor behind a structural outcome — the greedy executive, the lazy regulator, the feckless consumer. Sometimes there is one. Usually the villain is a role someone occupies and would be replaced in within a month.The second is subtler and, in practice, more dangerous: Moloch laundering. Because structural coercion is a real and respected phenomenon, claiming it is a cheap way to justify what you intended to do anyway. "We have to cut quality, or competitors will." "We can't be the only ones paying a living wage." "There is no alternative." Some of these claims are true. Many are not, and the tell is always the same.The test is not rhetorical. Ask: name the competitor who would take your customers, the mechanism by which you'd lose, and roughly how much. If that answer exists, you have a trap and should be designing an escape. If it dissolves into vagueness under questioning, you have a preference dressed as a constraint — which is the same move as smuggling a value premise in as a fact.A genuine trap, moreover, is falsifiable in the ordinary way. It predicts that players who restrain while others continue will lose ground measurably. Look for cases where someone actually did restrain unilaterally and check what happened. That is the difference between a structural claim and an alibi.No — and the distinction matters, because a blanket suspicion of competition is its own error. The same mechanism that produces Moloch produces most of the world's progress, and the difference lies entirely in the payoff structure. Productive competition escalates toward something whose benefits spill over: cheaper solar panels, better vaccines, faster chips, more accurate forecasts. The race is real, the losers lose, and the output is a shared gain. This is the "invisible hand" case — Adam Smith's mechanism producing a public benefit — and it is the same mechanism as a multipolar trap. Nothing about the market changed; the topology of who gains and who pays did. Positional competition escalates toward nothing. The resource is fixed, so effort is consumed without raising the total. This is the pure trap, and the diagnostic is simple: ask whether the escalation raises the aggregate or only the relative position. Evolution supplies the same spectrum: the peacock's tail and the Red Queen arms race between predator and prey are genuine traps in the individual-cost sense, and they are also where much of biological complexity came from. Some arms races build the world; some just burn it. The question is never "is this competitive?" but "who captures the benefit, and who absorbs the cost?"Every available exit attacks one of the three ingredients: it lowers the cost of contracting, it adds an enforcer, it changes the payoffs, or it changes the arena so the contested margin stops mattering.Reduce transaction costs. Traps require parties who cannot agree or cannot verify. Fewer players, well-defined rights, repeat interaction, and visibility all attack that. Repeat play is the single strongest lever: when the game is repeated and behaviour is observable, reputation does work that contracts cannot, which is the finding behind Robert Axelrod's tournaments on the iterated prisoner's dilemma — reciprocity succeeds, but only when the "shadow of the future" is long enough and defection is detectable. Making behaviour visible to the group is often all that is needed.Add an enforcer. Hobbes's answer, and the right one when parties are too numerous to bargain and detection is cheap: an authority that changes the payoffs by fiat. Treaties like the 1987 Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances, bans on growth-promotion antibiotics in livestock, and standardised charging ports are all examples of a third party internalising an externality that the market could not. The failure modes are equally instructive — the enforcer can be captured by those it regulates, can be too weak to detect violations, or can itself be caught in a race to the bottom with other jurisdictions.Change the payoffs. The cheapest escape and the hardest to build: norms, taboos, and internalised standards that make the defecting move costly to the person doing it, independent of enforcement. Professional ethics, queue discipline, and the refusal to bargain over certain things all work this way. This is also where religion and culture have historically done their heaviest lifting — not by explaining the trap, but by making one branch of it simply unavailable.Change the arena. Sometimes the contested margin can be removed rather than managed. Vertical integration internalises the externality by merging the players. A technological substitution can make the contested resource irrelevant — a new pricing mechanism, a substitute input, a design that removes the need for the scarce thing. Exit to a different game is a real strategy, and it is usually the one people forget to consider.Three cautions about the menu. First, escapes are themselves coordination problems: a cartel is an escape from a price war that must solve monitoring and sanctioning, which are the same problems it was trying to escape. Second, every fix creates new margins, and those margins will be found — the second-order effects chapter applies in full. Third, the level is not the goal. The question is not "how do we reduce advertising spending?" but "what is the structure we want, and who pays for it?" A trap broken by a rule that no one can renegotiate has traded one form of stuckness for another.Run this on any situation that feels like everyone is losing and no one is at fault: Name the agents and their moves. Who is choosing what, on what margin? Run the unilateral test. What exactly happens to one player who restrains while the others continue? If you cannot answer specifically, you have not found a trap. Find the externality. Whose cost is missing from whose payoff? That gap is the engine. Check the ratchet. Is the level rising over time, or is it static? A static bad equilibrium is a different problem — an unpleasant settlement rather than an escalation. Ask why contracting fails. Too many parties? Unverifiable behaviour? No trust? No enforcement? The answer names the escape. Ask whether it should be escaped. Does escalation buy a shared good, or only a relative position? Name the settlement. In the style of everything else in this book: state what you expect to change, by when, and what you would see if the trap has actually been broken rather than merely relabelled. The uncomfortable implication, and the reason this topic sits in the act on coordination, is that most of what looks like moral failure at scale is structural. People are not secretly worse than they appear; the incentives reach into ordinary decency and pull out the outcome nobody chose. That is bad news for anyone hoping to fix the world by exhortation. It is good news for anyone willing to work on the rules — because rules are the one thing in the picture that a small number of people can actually change.Multipolar trap — A situation in which multiple agents each have an incentive to take an action that is individually advantageous and collectively self-defeating, with no agent able to improve the outcome unilaterally.Moloch — Shorthand for the structure, rather than the perpetrator, behind traps; a metaphor drawn from Ginsberg's Howl and popularised by Scott Alexander. Names an outcome with no author, and is a mood rather than an explanation when invoked without a payoff structure.Prisoner's dilemma — The minimal two-player trap: a dominant move leading both players to a Pareto-dominated outcome they would both prefer to avoid.Dominant strategy — A move that yields a better payoff than the alternatives regardless of what others do.Nash equilibrium — An outcome in which no player can improve by changing strategy alone; it can be collectively terrible.Pareto-dominated / Pareto-superior — An outcome is Pareto-dominated when some alternative makes at least one party better off and none worse off; the alternative is Pareto-superior.Rivalrous and excludable — Two properties of a good: whether one person's use reduces what is available to others, and whether non-payers can be kept out. Traps live where a good is rivalrous but not excludable.Common-pool resource — A rivalrous, non-excludable resource — a fishery, aquifer, grazing range, or the atmosphere — where each user's extraction subtracts from every other user's supply.Externality — A cost or benefit of an action that falls on someone who did not choose it and is not party to any transaction with the actor. The missing term in the trap's payoff.Transaction costs — The costs of reaching, monitoring, and enforcing an agreement. High transaction costs among numerous parties are the reason traps cannot be bargained away.Escalation ratchet — The tendency of a trap's contested level to rise and stay risen, because the first party to step back down loses ground.Arms race — A trap in which competing parties escalate a capability whose value is largely relative, leaving all of them worse off in absolute terms.Race to the bottom — A trap in which jurisdictions or firms compete by lowering standards, each step justified by the competitive threat of the others.War of attrition / dollar auction — A trap of continued escalation over a single all-or-nothing prize, in which the rational calculation shifts from winning a gain to minimising a certain loss. Shubik's dollar auction is the canonical demonstration.Sunk cost — An unrecoverable prior expenditure; in a trap it changes the relative cost of quitting, which is a real accounting effect and not only a psychological error.Positional good — A good valued for one's rank relative to others; competition for it consumes resources without raising the total, producing escalation with no aggregate gain.Shadow of the future — Axelrod's term for the prospect of continued interaction; when it is long and behaviour is observable, reciprocity can sustain cooperation that a one-shot game destroys.Productive vs. positional competition — The distinction between escalation whose output everyone can use and escalation that only rearranges rank; the same competitive mechanism with opposite aggregate verdicts.Unilateral-restraint test — The practical diagnostic for distinguishing a structural trap from a rhetorical one: identify specifically what a player would lose by restraining alone. No specific loss, no trap.Moloch laundering — Invoking structural compulsion to justify a preference that would otherwise need defending; the failure mode of the concept in the hands of someone who already knows what they want to do.Enforcer (Leviathan) solution — Escaping a trap by introducing a third party with the power to change payoffs through regulation, mandate, or treaty; effective when parties are numerous and detection is cheap, vulnerable to capture and to its own competitive races.Capture — The condition in which the enforcing body comes to serve the interests of those it regulates, converting a solution into a new form of the problem.

item.title: 5-8 Moral luck + veil of ignorance
item.description: Part of 5 Act IV — The Coordination Problem (us)Two ideas from very different literatures turn out to be a diagnosis and a prescription. Moral luck is the discovery — by Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, in a 1976 volume of essays — that a great deal of what we praise and blame people for depends on factors they did not control. The veil of ignorance is John Rawls's design response: if position is so often an accident, then rules should be chosen by people who do not yet know which position they will occupy. Read together, they give you one of the few genuinely portable tools in this book: a test for whether a rule you are about to impose is one you would accept from underneath.The control principle is the moral intuition almost everyone holds and almost nobody can consistently apply: you are morally assessable only for what is within your control. It underwrites "ought implies can," the excuse of accident, and the difference between a mistake and a crime. Kant built it into the foundations of ethics, and ordinary moral practice assumes it continuously.Nagel's argument is that almost nothing survives it. He distinguishes four places luck gets in, and they form a chain from who you are to what you did: Constitutive luck — your temperament, talents, capacity for courage or sympathy. Nobody chose to be born patient or quick-tempered. Circumstantial luck — the situations you happen to face. The same person born in Nuremberg in 1920 and in Buenos Aires in 1920 lived under different moral demands. One had the opportunity to be a hero or a collaborator; the other mostly had the opportunity to be unremarkable. Causal luck — how your actions were caused, which is where this runs into the free-will problem. Nagel sets it aside as the deepest case; it is not needed for the argument to bite. Resultant luck — how things turned out. This is the one that disturbs moral practice most, because it is visible every day. Worked example. Two drivers leave the same pub over the legal limit. Both are equally reckless, equally impaired, equally fortunate in their cars and reflexes. One gets home. The other, at exactly the same speed and reaction time, meets a child who steps into the road half a second earlier. The first driver has a story; the second has a manslaughter conviction, a lifetime of guilt, and a permanent place in the moral record. Nothing that distinguishes them is something either one controlled. We can feel the unfairness and we still — courtrooms, newspapers, and the drivers themselves — treat them as different people.Williams's contribution is a second, subtler case. His example is a lorry driver who, through no fault whatever, kills a child who runs out in front of him. He is not morally guilty. But Williams argues he nonetheless owes a special kind of response — agent-regret — precisely because it was his lorry and his hands on the wheel. It is not ordinary regret (which anyone might feel) and not guilt (which would presume fault). It is the first-person residue of having been the vehicle of a catastrophe, and telling the driver "you did nothing wrong" does not dissolve it. Moral luck therefore contaminates not only how others judge you but how you must judge yourself.The result is what Nagel called an antinomy: two things we cannot give up, which cannot both be true. We cannot abandon the control principle without turning morality into a lottery. We cannot abandon our practices of praise, blame, and punishment without abandoning moral life altogether. Nagel's honest conclusion is that this is not a puzzle with a clever solution; it is a structural feature of morality that we mostly paper over.You cannot dissolve moral luck, but you can act on the knowledge that it exists, and the payoff is mostly institutional.Separate blame from liability. Blame is retrospective: it asks what you deserve, and it is contaminated by luck. Liability is forward-looking: it asks who should bear a cost, and it is a design question. A hospital can require a surgeon whose patient died to undergo review — because review reduces future deaths — while declining to assert that she is a worse person than a colleague whose identical patient survived. Consequence and condemnation are separate judgements that habit fuses.Assess process where you can, outcome where you must. Outcome-based judgement is the source of resultant luck and of survivorship bias; purely process-based judgement loses the discipline that makes care matter, and invites the failure mode where the metric replaces the goal. Most good systems mix: judge the process contemporaneously, judge the outcome only across many cases where the noise averages out.Expect the just-world reflex. People have a strong tendency to infer desert from outcome — the successful must have deserved it, the unlucky must have done something. This is a comfort mechanism that makes the world feel ordered, and it is wrong in exactly the way survivorship bias is wrong. It is also the main reason the veil of ignorance feels counterintuitive to people who are well placed: if your position is earned, there is no reason to choose rules without knowing it.Rawls's original position is a thought experiment about how to choose the basic rules of a society. Parties in it are rational, mutually disinterested, and choosing principles to govern their shared institutions — but they choose behind a veil of ignorance. They do not know their class, their natural talents, their family, their conception of the good, or which generation they belong to. They know general facts about economics and psychology; they do not know who they are.It is worth being precise about what this device is. It is not a state of nature, not a bargaining session, and not a claim about how societies began. It is a device of representation: a way of modelling the requirement that a rule not be tailored to advantage whoever happens to be writing it. Rawls's phrase for what it screens out is that the distribution of benefits should not be settled by factors "arbitrary from a moral point of view."The mechanism is straightforward. If you do not know whether you will be the landlord or the tenant, the healthy or the ill, the majority or the minority, then self-interest no longer tells you to write a rule for the strong. Rawls argued that parties so situated would choose two principles: equal basic liberties for all, and social and economic inequalities permitted only when they also improve the position of the worst off — the difference principle.That conclusion is contested, and one objection is worth knowing because it defines the tool's sensitivity. John Harsanyi argued that if the parties are genuinely ignorant, they should assign equal probability to each position and maximize average utility — a straightforward expected-value calculation. Rawls's parties instead reason as if the worst outcome is the one that matters, which is maximin. The two produce different societies. Which is right depends on what you assume about the choosers' attitude to risk — which means the veil does not generate answers by itself. It relocates disagreement from "what should we do?" to "what would reasonable people behind the veil agree to?" — a better question, but still a question.Most people will never settle the Harsanyi–Rawls dispute, and do not need to. The practical value of the veil is that it is a fast consistency check on any rule you are about to impose, and it can be run in a few minutes.Step three is the one people skip and the one that does the work. You cannot run the test without naming the affected population and identifying the worst position in it — which is why the veil is a useful complement to baselines and base rates: it forces you to look at the tail rather than the typical case.Worked example: a firm's layoff rule. A company needs to cut 10% of costs. Option A: lay off the 10% with the weakest performance reviews. Option B: a 10% pay cut across the board, no layoffs. Option C: reduce the dividend and the executive bonus pool first, then a smaller pay cut.Run the veil. Population: employees, shareholders, customers. Positions: top performer with a mortgage, middling performer with a sick parent, recent hire, long-tenured specialist whose role has been automated, shareholder, customer. Worst positions: the worker laid off in a weak local job market, and the worker whose pay falls below what the household needs. Behind the veil, not knowing which you are, Option A looks like a lottery over ruin; Option C concentrates the pain where it is most survivable. Notice that the tool has not told you that layoffs are wrong. It has told you that if you would not accept a rule knowing you might be the one it destroys, you owe an argument for why not — an actual argument, not the observation that it is efficient.Worked example: drought pricing. A water utility must cut consumption by 20%. Option A: a flat restriction on all households. Option B: steeply rising per-litre prices. Option C: a free allocation per person, with trading above it. Behind the veil, you do not know whether you are a large household, a small one, a landlord passing costs to tenants, or a business whose competitors are in the next jurisdiction. Option B's burden falls hardest on people for whom water is a large share of the budget; Option C preserves the signal while capping the damage; Option A ignores that the same litre means different things to different households. Again the tool produces a critique rather than a verdict — and the critique is where the useful argument starts.Three honest limits.You can smuggle yourself back in. Whoever specifies the parties — their risk aversion, their preferences, whether they care about future generations — determines much of the answer. A person who wants low taxes can populate the original position with parties who happen to dislike redistribution. The veil is a consistency check, not an oracle; it detects rules that advantaged their author, and it cannot manufacture agreement where values genuinely differ.The boundary problem is unresolved. Who gets a seat behind the veil? Rawls's own treatment of future generations is notoriously awkward, and non-human interests and outsiders who never get to negotiate fit poorly. Every real application involves drawing a line that some affected party does not get to help draw.It does not generate compliance. Knowing what a fair rule is does not make anyone follow it, which is why moral luck and the veil both sit inside an act about coordination rather than an act about knowledge. Fairness arguments operate on people who are already persuaded; the rest is institutions, incentives, and the multipolar traps covered elsewhere in this act.Moral luck is the empirical claim; the veil is the procedural response. If a large share of your position, your character, and your outcomes is not your doing, then a rule chosen by people who know they hold the good position will encode an accident as a desert.The link is not merely thematic. It explains why the veil is politically unstable: it asks people to reason as though their advantages were contingent, and the just-world reflex — reinforced by every survivorship-biased success story they have ever read — tells them the opposite. It also explains what the veil is for. It is not a machine for producing just institutions. It is a machine for catching the moment when you were about to write your own position into a rule and call it neutral. That is a smaller claim than Rawls's, and it is one you can use this afternoon. Severance and restructuring — choosing a layoff rule behind the veil rather than defending the one that protects you. Sentencing and liability — the drunk driver example, generalized: outcome-based penalties when outcomes are noisy. Insurance and credit — pricing that is actuarially accurate and veil-unacceptable, and the reverse. Algorithmic systems — the appeal procedure matters more than the model, because you do not know whether you will be the one who needs it. Disaster relief and pandemic policy — rules written before you know which neighbourhood you live in. Admissions, funding, and promotion — where the assessor's own path is the unexamined template. Family and team rules — the same test at small scale, where it is cheapest to run and most often skipped. State the rule as a rule, not as a decision. Name everyone affected, including people who cannot speak in the decision. List the positions and identify the worst one. Ask whether you would accept the rule without knowing which position is yours. If not, name what would have to change — a floor, a compensation, a different rule — and then ask what your actual objection was. Step five is where the honesty lives. Often the answer is that you would accept the rule, and you simply prefer your current position to be protected. That is a legitimate thing to want, but it is a value claim, not a fairness claim, and it belongs on the table as one.Moral luck — The phenomenon that a person's moral record depends substantially on factors beyond their control; Nagel's and Williams's term for the tension this creates with the control principle.Control principle — The intuition that agents are morally assessable only for what they could control; the assumption moral luck undermines.Constitutive luck — Luck in who one is: temperament, capacities, and dispositions that shape action without being chosen.Circumstantial luck — Luck in the situations and moral demands one happens to face; the reason the same person can have radically different moral records in different times and places.Causal luck — Luck in how one's actions were caused; the free-will dimension of the problem.Resultant luck — Luck in how an action turned out; the source of the drunk-driver asymmetry and of outcome-based blame generally.Agent-regret (Williams) — The special first-person response of someone who, though blameless, was the vehicle of a harm; not guilt, and not dissolved by being told one is blameless.Antinomy (of moral luck) — The unresolvable conflict between the control principle and ordinary moral practice; Nagel's claim is that it has no clean solution.Just-world tendency — The inclination to infer desert from outcome, so that the successful and the unlucky are assumed to have earned their positions; the main psychological obstacle to veil reasoning.Original position (Rawls) — The hypothetical choice situation in which parties select principles of justice for their society.Veil of ignorance — The restriction in the original position that parties do not know their own class, talents, family, or conception of the good; a device for preventing rules from being tailored to their author's position.Device of representation — Rawls's description of the original position: not a historical or psychological claim, but a way of modelling impartiality.Difference principle — Rawls's claim that inequalities are just only if they also improve the position of the worst-off group.Maximin — The decision rule of choosing the option whose worst outcome is least bad; Rawls's characterization of choice behind the veil.Harsanyi's objection — The argument that genuinely ignorant parties should assign equal probabilities across positions and maximize average utility, yielding a different (broadly utilitarian) conclusion than Rawls's maximin.Arbitrary from a moral point of view — Rawls's phrase for the natural and social contingencies — birth, talent, family — that should not determine distributive outcomes.Smuggling — The failure mode in which the person specifying the parties behind the veil encodes their own preferences into the parties' preferences, making the device yield the answer they already wanted.
